Verified two independent ways: (a) constructive build asserting every one of the 73 bytes is covered by exactly one breakdown entry, (b) an independently written BER walker that re-parses the hex with no overrun and no trailing bytes. Every length field here is SHORT form (max 71) — that is the trap: the same document must emit long form for the response.

captures.notes: Chosen legal values, stated explicitly: sysDescr is a real-shape Cisco IOS 12.x/15.x banner, chosen at 247 bytes specifically so the packet exercises BOTH multi-byte length forms in one capture — 0x81 (one length octet) on the OCTET STRING at offset 49, and 0x82 (two length octets) on all four enclosing constructed nodes. TimeTicks 9740722 = 27h 3m 27s uptime, chosen so its top significant byte is 0x94 and the mandatory unsigned 0x00 pad appears. Verified the same two ways as the request: full-coverage assertion over all 337 bytes, plus an independent BER walker (no overrun, no trailing). NOTE the width profile: request length fields are (1,1,1,1,1) octets at the five nesting levels; response is (2,3,3,3,3). Same message shape, different field widths — this is the core hazard.

statefulness:
SNMPv2c looks stateless and therefore looks easy for §5. That is a trap: the protocol has no SESSION state, so the state model as designed (states, transitions, requires-chaining, conflicts) degenerates to a single "ready" state with an empty transition list and nothing to say — while all of SNMP's real state sits in places §5 has no vocabulary for. Six specific demands:

1. LEGAL-MESSAGE-PER-STATE — vacuous, and that is the finding. There is no connect, no login, no session token. The community string is a bearer credential retransmitted in full on every single message (offset 5-12 of the request, 7-14 of the response). So `validIn:["authenticated"]` and `requires:["login"]` never bind to anything. Nothing in the protocol is illegal in any state. §5's per-message constraints are dead weight here, and a model that can only express session-shaped state will silently model this protocol as trivial when it is not.

2. WHAT MUST CHAIN — not messages, but ITERATIONS. The chaining unit in SNMP is the walk: response N's last returned OID becomes request N+1's requested OID, and the loop ends on a data condition (returned OID leaves the requested subtree, or a varbind value carries the endOfMibView marker, tag 0x82 zero-length). §4's back edges cap out at `loop:{max:n}, n <= 64` constant, so the single most common SNMP operation is inexpressible. That is a chaining requirement the model cannot state at all, not merely one it states poorly.

3. WHAT MUST NEVER COMBINE — `conflicts` has no scope to attach to. Without a session there is no container whose lifetime bounds "never in the same session". The real constraints are time-and-device-scoped: do not SET a table while walking it (rows shift under you and you get a torn read); do not run two walks of the same table concurrently; do not retransmit a non-idempotent SET without dedup. `conflicts` needs `{"scope":"device","windowMs":n}` to mean anything here.

4. CONCURRENCY — §5 is one FSM per (protocol, device). A manager keeps many GETs in flight on ONE UDP socket, distinguished solely by request-id (my capture: 821915, echoed byte-exact at response offset 21). §4's `expect` correlation on `token` matches one reply correctly, but there is no per-request state container, no outstanding-request table, and no max-outstanding bound. Add an `instance.*` scope keyed by request-id.

5. CONFIRMED vs PRESUMED — inverted from §5's assumed shape. For GET everything is CONFIRMED observation, but every observation is a SNAPSHOT with a TTL and, critically, is valid only for one agent incarnation. sysUpTime.0 (my varbind 2, TimeTicks 9740722 at offset 312) is that incarnation clock. §5's presume/confidence/ttl machinery handles "we wrote it, we presume it stuck" — the SET case, where `confirmedBy` genuinely fits, though it confirms one message with one match expression while an SNMP SET is a list of varbinds that agents are supposed to apply atomically and frequently do not, so a partial SET leaves you presuming N values when k took. What §5 has no vocabulary for is the GET case: an observation whose validity is scoped to an epoch that a LATER observation can retroactively revoke.

6. WHERE YOU ONLY LEARN FROM THE NEXT RESPONSE — three cases, in increasing order of nastiness.
 (a) Credential/reachability failure is INVISIBLE. A wrong community produces no reply at all (the agent discards the PDU and bumps snmpInBadCommunityNames). That is byte-identical to host-down, UDP/161 filtered, source-IP ACL rejection, agent not listening, and packet loss. §5's `onTimeout:"<state>"` forces exactly one conclusion, and every available conclusion is unsound. The model needs an indeterminate outcome — "we learned nothing" as a first-class result with a consistent-with set — because in this protocol silence is the primary failure signal and negative evidence is not evidence. §5 currently assumes every message either succeeds or fails informatively; SNMPv2c's dominant failure mode is neither.
 (b) Session-equivalent death is detected by counter regression. If sysUpTime comes back SMALLER than last poll, the agent restarted: counters reset to zero, ifIndex assignments may have been renumbered, and every fact from before that moment is unsound. This is §5's "state discovered by failure" idea, except the discovery is not an error code — it is a monotonic value going backwards, and the required response is retroactive invalidation of a whole class of previously-emitted facts. `implies` keys off `capture.*` only and can invalidate named session values; it cannot compare capture to `store.*` and cannot invalidate fact globs.
 (c) The worst case: wrong state manifests as CORRECT-LOOKING DATA. After an ifIndex renumber, a GET of ifDescr.5 returns a perfectly well-formed value for a different interface. No error status, no exception marker, no timeout — just a silently wrong answer that will be emitted as a fact with full confidence. Every mechanism in §5 keys off an error signal (`capture.status == 401`). There is no signal. The only defence is an identity anchor re-checked every poll (ifDescr/ifName/entPhysicalSerialNum) plus the epoch guard from (b), and expressing that needs `implies` to compare capture against persisted state.

Also worth naming under statefulness because it is state-shaped rather than field-shaped: tooBig(1) returns an EMPTY varbind list, so a too-large poll yields no data and no indication of which varbind was at fault — the correct behaviour is to split the request and retry recursively, a response-directed narrowing retry that neither the static edge set nor §5 can express. And the exception markers noSuchObject/noSuchInstance/endOfMibView are PER-VARBIND, so a single response is simultaneously a success and a failure at element granularity while §5 models outcome only per message.

Net: of §5's seven self-declared known gaps, SNMPv2c independently confirms four (negotiated capability — v1/v2c/v3 probing where every negative result is silence; retransmission/dedup — UDP with request-id reuse; decoder-carried state — the BER region stack; and, in the tooBig sense, fragmentation) and adds four the list does not have: indeterminate outcomes, epoch/generation invalidation, concurrent operation instances, and element-granular outcomes.

gaps.what: BER definite-length fields are variable-width and self-sizing. v0's only length primitives are fixed-width scalars (`{"u8":"len(group:X)"}`), and §3's two-pass rule explicitly says pass 1 emits "a placeholder of the declared width". BER has no declared width.
gaps.why: Measured on my two captures, the five nested length fields are (1,1,1,1,1) octets in the request and (2,3,3,3,3) in the response. Response offset 1 is `82 01 4d` and offset 49 is `81 f7`. Worse, the width feeds back: I searched sysDescr lengths 100..300 and every one of nine boundaries (n=100->101, 113->114, 115->116, 127->128, 211->212, 225->226, 239->240, 242->243, 255->256) grows the packet by +2 for a +1 payload byte, because a length field crossed a width boundary and its extra octet is itself counted by every enclosing length. A single back-patch pass over fixed-width placeholders cannot converge on this; the placeholder's own size is part of the answer.

gaps.what: No OBJECT IDENTIFIER converter. §6's converter set is explicitly closed.
gaps.why: 1.3.6.1.4.1.2021.10.1.3.1 must become `2b 06 01 04 01 8f 65 0a 01 03 01`. Two rules defeat every available converter: (a) the first two arcs merge as 40*1+3 = 43 = 0x2b, so the output has one fewer element than the input; (b) each remaining arc is base-128 with bit 7 set on all but the last octet — arc 2021 becomes `8f 65` — so arcs are 1..5 octets. `split` gives a List<Text>; there is no fold, no while, and `each` produces one field group per item with no way to vary that group's byte count by the item's magnitude. `dnsName` is the only structural converter in the table and it is label-length-prefixed, not base-128.
gaps.proposedFix:
Two converters:
  oid    : Text -> Bytes   ("1.3.6.1.2.1.1.1.0" -> 2b 06 01 02 01 01 01 00; applies 40*x+y and base-128)
  unoid  : Bytes -> Text   (inverse)
And, because they are useful independently (protobuf, MIDI, ASN.1 tag numbers >30, DWARF):
  base128 / unbase128 : Int <-> Bytes
Register accepted/produced kinds so §6's validate-time type checking still holds. `oid` round-trips exactly, because BER forbids non-minimal arc encodings (a leading 0x80 octet is illegal) — so unlike GAP-3 this converter is lossless in both directions.

gaps.what: No minimal two's-complement INTEGER converter, and no unsigned-minimal variant for the SNMP APPLICATION types.
gaps.why: request-id 821915 must encode as `02 03 0c 8a 9b` — length 3. `i32be` emits 4 octets (`00 0c 8a 9b`), which is both the wrong bytes and the wrong declared length. Symmetrically, TimeTicks 9740722 must be `43 04 00 94 a1 b2`: it is UNSIGNED, so a 0x00 pad octet is mandatory because 0x94 has bit 7 set, but for TimeTicks 5 the answer is `43 01 05`. So the same field is 1..5 octets depending on the value, and signed and unsigned differ on the pad. No fixed-width scalar can produce either.
gaps.proposedFix:
derInt    : Int -> Bytes   (minimal two's-complement, signed: strip redundant 00/ff leading octets, keep one if the sign bit would flip)
  unDerInt  : Bytes -> Int
  derUint   : Int -> Bytes   (non-negative, prepend 0x00 iff bit 7 of the top significant octet is set)
  unDerUint : Bytes -> Int
These pair with GAP-1's berLen so `{"tlv":{"t":"u8","l":"berLen","v":"inputs.requestId | derInt"}}` emits the whole TLV. Note honestly: derInt is NOT a byte-exact inverse of unDerInt over all legal BER input — see GAP-11.

gaps.what: Decode mode has no field that captures N bytes where N is a runtime value.
gaps.why: §3's decode example offers only scalars, `skip`, and `each`. To read the 6-byte community, the 8- and 11-byte OIDs, and the 247-byte sysDescr, the byte count comes from a length field just read. `{"skip":"capture.commLen"}` advances but discards. `{"each":"capture.commLen","fields":[{"u8":null}],"as":"x"}` yields List<Int>, and no converter in §6 turns List<Int> into Bytes or Text (`ascii`/`latin1` are Text->Bytes; `concat` is unspecified over List<Int>). The encode-side `{"value":expr,"repeat":n}` might be read as a decode-mode N-byte capture under §3's "same field list" rule, but `repeat` on encode means "repeat the encoded value n times", not "read n bytes" — so that reading is a spec ambiguity, not a feature. Result: the community string of even the SIMPLE request is uncapturable.
gaps.proposedFix:
{ "bytes": { "len": "capture.commLen" }, "as":"community", "conv":"latin1" }
with `"len"` also accepting the sentinels "remaining" (to end of the enclosing region, see GAP-7) and "rest" (to end of input). Mirror it on encode as { "bytes": { "of":"inputs.community | ascii" } } so the field list stays symmetric, which is §3's stated invariant.

gaps.what: Decode has no repeat-until-end-of-region. `each` takes a count expression.
gaps.why: The VarBindList contains three varbinds, but 3 appears nowhere on the wire. The count is implied by the enclosing length (303) being exhausted, and the items are 264, 18 and 21 bytes, so the count is not derivable arithmetically either (contrast §3's Modbus example, `capture.byteCount / 2`, which only works because registers are fixed-size). This is the single most common shape in the protocol — an SNMP walk returns a list of unknown length in every response.
gaps.proposedFix:
{ "each": { "until":"endOfRegion" }, "as":"varBinds", "fields":[ ... ] }
with siblings `{"until":"endOfInput"}` and `{"until":"<expr>"}` plus a mandatory `"max": n` guard so the packet/work bound §4 cares about stays computable. Requires GAP-7's region stack to give `endOfRegion` a meaning.

gaps.what: No tag dispatch / discriminated union. The parse tree's SHAPE depends on a byte just read.
gaps.why: A varbind's value type is carried in its ASN.1 tag: 0x04 OCTET STRING, 0x02 INTEGER, 0x06 OID, 0x40 IpAddress, 0x41 Counter32, 0x42 Gauge32, 0x43 TimeTicks, 0x46 Counter64, and the zero-length exception markers 0x80 noSuchObject / 0x81 noSuchInstance / 0x82 endOfMibView. My response carries 0x04 and 0x43 in the same list. Each demands a different converter. The same hazard hits the request-id, whose scalar width (u8/u16be/u24be/u32be) must be chosen from `capture.reqIdLen` at runtime. §3's `when` is only ever shown on encode fields, and even granting it in decode, `when` is inclusion/exclusion, not an n-way dispatch that binds one capture name to differently-typed results.
gaps.proposedFix:
{ "switch": "capture.valueTag",
  "cases": { "0x04": [ {"bytes":{"len":"remaining"},"as":"value","conv":"latin1"} ],
             "0x43": [ {"bytes":{"len":"remaining"},"as":"value","conv":"unDerUint"} ],
             "0x80": [ {"set":"valueKind","to":"'noSuchObject'"} ] },
  "default": [ {"bytes":{"len":"remaining"},"as":"value"} ] }
plus `"captureTagAs":"valueTag"` on `tlv` so the tag byte is bound before the switch runs. On encode the same node selects a case by `"on":"inputs.valueKind"`, keeping the field list symmetric.

gaps.what: No bounded sub-decode region. A length field covers a span that itself contains length fields, and the decoder must carry that bound down and across siblings.
gaps.why: Response offset 31 declares vbl = 303 bytes; the three varbinds inside must consume exactly 303, and vb1's own 260 must be consumed exactly by its OID TLV plus its value TLV. Decoding is therefore not a pure per-field fold over a single cursor — it needs a stack of (start, limit) frames, an overrun error when a child exceeds its parent, and an underrun error when a parent's bytes are left unconsumed. This is the same class as §5's acknowledged "decoder-carried state" gap (CoAP option delta, DNS compression), which confirms the gap is structural rather than protocol-specific.

gaps.what: `tlv` / `tlvList` values are opaque expressions, not nested field lists — so there is no recursion, and no way to sub-parse a captured byte range.
gaps.why: §3 defines `{"tlv":{"t":"u8","l":"u8","v":"inputs.opts"}}`. `v` is a byte blob. BER is recursive by construction: my response nests Message > PDU > VarBindList > VarBind > value, five levels, and a varbind value may itself be an OID (tag 0x06) or, in other PDUs, an Opaque wrapping a whole further BER document. With `v` opaque you can neither build a structured value nor feed a captured blob back into another parse block. `l:"u8"` also hard-codes the short form (GAP-1).

gaps.what: Span names inside `each` are not iteration-scoped, so `len(group:vb)` inside a loop is ambiguous.
gaps.why: My three varbinds each need their own length (12, 12, 15 in the request; 260, 16, 19 in the response). The document declares `{"group":"vb", ...}` once inside `{"each":"inputs.oids"}`, so it is instantiated three times. §3 says a group is "a named span — referenceable by len()", singular. Either the name collides (validation error) or it silently resolves to one arbitrary instance — and §3's promise that cyclic/unresolvable spans are "a validation error, never a runtime failure" cannot be kept if the engine has to guess.
gaps.proposedFix: Specify that a `group` declared inside an `each` body creates one span per iteration, and that `len(group:X)` lexically inside the same body binds to the current iteration's instance. Add explicit escapes for the other two intents: `len(group:X@i)` for a specific iteration and `len(group:X@all)` for the concatenation. This is a scoping rule in the expression resolver, not new machinery.

gaps.what: `each ... as:"r"` binds a scalar, and `inputs` types top out at `list<T>` over scalars. A varbind is a record.
gaps.why: Encoding the GetResponse means iterating over [{oid:"1.3.6.1.2.1.1.1.0", type:"OctetString", value:"Cisco IOS..."}, {oid:"1.3.6.1.2.1.1.3.0", type:"TimeTicks", value:9740722}, ...]. §3's example binds `r` and uses it whole (`{"u16be":"r"}`); §6's type list has no object/record and the path list has no member access, so `r.oid` and `r.type` are not legal expressions. Every real SNMP response, and every SET request, is a list of records.
gaps.proposedFix:
Add a structured input type and member access on the iteration binding:
  { "name":"varBinds", "kind":"prompt", "type":"list<record>",
    "schema": { "oid":"text", "type":"enum", "value":"text" },
    "description":"..." }
and permit `r.<field>` wherever `r` is legal today. Also add `r.$index` (0-based) and `r.$ordinal` (1-based), which GAP-19 needs for error-index.

gaps.what: Non-canonical-but-legal BER is unrecoverable, so encode(decode(bytes)) is not byte-exact in general. The grammar has no way to record the encoding form it observed.
gaps.why: BER (unlike DER) permits a long-form length where short form would do — `30 81 47` instead of `30 47` — and permits non-minimal INTEGER padding — `02 04 00 0c 8a 9b` instead of `02 03 0c 8a 9b`. Both occur in the field: several embedded agents and some Windows SNMP stacks emit long-form lengths unconditionally, and a manager is required to accept them. My unDerInt/derInt pair maps both `02 03 0c 8a 9b` and `02 04 00 0c 8a 9b` to the Int 821915, and re-encodes both as the 3-octet form. The bytes on the wire are then not the bytes that came in — which matters because SNMPv3 authentication (HMAC over the received message) and any capture-replay test are byte-sensitive. This is a genuine ambiguity, and it is a finding, not a bug I can fix in the document.

gaps.what: §4 caps back edges at `loop:{max:n}`, n a constant <= 64. That makes an SNMP walk — the single most common SNMP operation — inexpressible.
gaps.why: GETNEXT/GETBULK walking ifTable or ipRouteTable on a real switch is hundreds to tens of thousands of iterations. Worse, termination is data-driven, not count-driven: you stop when the returned OID is no longer prefixed by the requested subtree, or when the value carries the endOfMibView marker (tag 0x82, zero length). A constant bound of 64 cannot express either. And each iteration's request OID comes from the previous response, so it is a genuine feedback loop, not an unrolled sequence.
gaps.proposedFix:
Replace the constant iteration cap with a resource budget plus a data-driven exit:
  "loop": { "until": "capture.varBinds[-1].valueKind == 'endOfMibView' || !(capture.varBinds[-1].oid | startsWith(inputs.subtree))",
            "maxPackets": 4096, "maxMillis": 60000, "maxBytes": 4194304 }
The packet bound §4 wants to keep computable is still computable — it is now stated directly as maxPackets rather than inferred from a constant iteration count, which is strictly more honest for a loop whose body sends one packet.

gaps.what: The state model cannot represent "we learned nothing". `onTimeout` forces a single interpretation of silence, and in SNMPv2c silence is the ONLY failure signal for the most important failure.
gaps.why: A wrong community string produces no reply at all — RFC 3416 agents silently discard the PDU and increment snmpInBadCommunityNames. That is byte-for-byte indistinguishable from: host down, UDP/161 filtered, agent not listening, agent's ACL rejecting our source IP, response lost, or response too big to route. §5 offers `"connected": { "timeoutMs":30000, "onTimeout":"disconnected" }` — one destination state, i.e. one asserted conclusion. Any conclusion drawn here is unsound. There is also no negative-evidence concept in `emits`: you cannot record "community 'public' is NOT confirmed" as distinct from "community 'public' is wrong".
gaps.proposedFix:
Make timeout produce ambiguity rather than a transition:
  "onTimeout": { "outcome":"indeterminate",
                 "consistentWith":["badCommunity","unreachable","filtered","lost"],
                 "state":"unchanged" }
and allow an emitted fact to carry confidence "unknown" so a probe can record that it ran without asserting a result. Add a discriminator hook so a later observation can collapse the set:
  "discriminatedBy": [ { "probe":"icmpEcho", "onOk":"eliminate:unreachable" } ]
This is the sharpest state-model finding in the protocol: the model currently assumes every message either succeeds or fails informatively, and SNMPv2c's dominant failure mode is neither.

gaps.what: No representation of multiple concurrent in-flight requests. `model` is one global FSM per (protocol, device); SNMP correlation is per-request-id and several are outstanding at once on one socket.
gaps.why: A manager routinely has 5-50 GETs in flight on a single UDP socket, distinguished only by request-id. There is no connection to hang session state on. §4's `expect` correlation on `token` handles matching ONE reply, but §5's states/transitions/`conflicts` are all session-scoped, and SNMPv2c has no session for them to scope to — so `"conflicts":["firmwareUpdate"]` has no lifetime to attach to and is silently vacuous. Layered on that: UDP retransmission reuses the same request-id, so a retransmit plus a late original yields two replies to one logical request (the acknowledged "retransmission + dedup window" gap, confirmed here concretely).
gaps.proposedFix:
Give operations instance scope and give `conflicts` an explicit lifetime:
  "correlation": { "key":"requestId", "scope":"instance", "maxOutstanding":16,
                   "dedupWindowMs":5000, "retransmit":{ "afterMs":1000, "max":3, "reuseKey":true } }
  "conflicts": [ { "message":"snmpSet", "scope":"device", "windowMs":5000 } ]
Add an `instance.*` expression scope (sibling to state/session/store/seq) holding per-request state, so a reply can be attributed and a duplicate dropped without a per-protocol code path.

gaps.what: No response-directed narrowing retry. SNMP's tooBig(1) demands re-issuing the same message with a subset of its inputs.
gaps.why: If the GetResponse would exceed the agent's maxMsgSize (often 1472 bytes to avoid IP fragmentation), RFC 3416 has the agent return error-status = tooBig(1) with an EMPTY variable-bindings list — so you get no data at all and no indication of which varbind was the problem. My response is already 337 bytes for three varbinds; a 40-varbind poll routinely trips this. Correct behaviour is to split the varbind list and retry, recursively. §4's edges are static and §5 has no retry primitive; expressing "halve the input list and re-send" needs a step that rewrites its own inputs.
gaps.proposedFix:
{ "id":"reply", "kind":"expect",
  "retry": [ { "when":"capture.errorStatus == 1",
               "resend":"snmpV2cGet",
               "with": { "inputs.oids":"inputs.oids | take(len(inputs.oids) / 2)" },
               "then":"resume", "max":6 } ] }
The same primitive covers CoAP 4.13 Request Entity Too Large and HTTP 413, so it generalises beyond SNMP.

gaps.what: No epoch/generation guard. An agent restart silently invalidates every previously cached fact, and the only evidence is a counter going backwards in a LATER response.
gaps.why: sysUpTime.0 (my varbind 2, value 9740722) is the agent's incarnation clock. If the next poll returns a SMALLER sysUpTime, the agent restarted: all Counter32/Counter64 values reset, ifIndex assignments may have been renumbered, and every fact derived from an earlier poll is now unsound. §5's `implies` keys off the current capture only (`capture.status == 401`) and can invalidate named session values; it cannot compare capture to `store.*`, and it cannot retroactively invalidate a class of facts learned from earlier messages. This is the worst failure mode in the protocol because wrong state manifests as plausible, well-formed, correct-looking data — ifDescr.5 simply returns a different interface, and nothing errors.
gaps.proposedFix:
Allow `implies` to compare capture against persisted state and to invalidate fact globs:
  "implies": [ { "when":"capture.sysUpTime < store.lastSysUpTime",
                 "invalidate":["dev.snmp.*", "dev.if.*"],
                 "set":{ "store.epoch":"store.epoch + 1" } },
               { "when":"capture.ifDescr != store.ifDescr", "invalidate":["dev.if.*"] } ]
and stamp every emitted fact with `store.epoch` so stale-epoch facts are dropped rather than merged. This generalises to any device with a boot counter or a reconfiguration generation.

gaps.what: No wrap-aware delta primitive for Counter32/Counter64, whose absolute value is meaningless.
gaps.why: A Counter32 (tag 0x41) reading is only useful as (v2-v1)/(t2-t1), with a 2^32 wrap correction, and is invalid across the epoch change of the previous gap. `store.*` can hold the previous sample, but §6 has no wrap-aware subtraction and no way to mark the first observation as producing no fact.
gaps.proposedFix:
delta32(prev)      : Int -> Int   (wrap-corrected difference modulo 2^32; yields null on the first observation)
  delta64(prev)      : Int -> Int
  rate(prev, prevAt) : Int -> Int   (per-second)
Used as `capture.ifInOctets | delta32(store.prevInOctets)`. A null result must suppress the `emits` binding rather than emit zero.

gaps.what: Per-element outcomes. One GetResponse is simultaneously a success and a failure, per varbind, and `emits` is per-message.
gaps.why: noSuchObject (tag 0x80), noSuchInstance (0x81) and endOfMibView (0x82) are zero-length exception VALUES inside individual varbinds, not error-status codes. A response can carry two good values and one noSuchInstance with error-status = 0 (noError). The right outcome is: emit two facts, and emit a distinct negative fact "this object is absent on this device" for the third — which is genuinely useful for capability discovery. §5 models message-level success/failure only.
gaps.proposedFix:
Let `emits` iterate and filter, and let it emit absence:
  "emits": [ { "each":"capture.varBinds", "as":"vb",
               "when":"vb.valueKind == 'value'", "fact":"dev.snmp.oid(vb.oid)", "from":"vb.value" },
             { "each":"capture.varBinds", "as":"vb",
               "when":"vb.valueKind == 'noSuchObject'",
               "fact":"dev.snmp.absent(vb.oid)", "value":true, "confidence":"confirmed" } ]

gaps.what: No list indexing in expressions, so error-index cannot be resolved and `emits` cannot address a captured element.
gaps.why: error-index is a 1-based index into the varbind list naming which varbind caused a PDU-level failure. Resolving it means `capture.varBinds[capture.errorIndex - 1].oid`. §6's path list (`inputs.* consts.* device.* capture.* ...`) shows no indexing and no negative indexing, yet a walk's loop condition needs `capture.varBinds[-1].oid` (the last returned OID becomes the next request's OID).
gaps.proposedFix: Add indexing to path resolution: `capture.varBinds[0]`, `capture.varBinds[-1]`, and `capture.varBinds[capture.errorIndex - 1]`, with an out-of-range index resolving to null rather than erroring (null then suppresses the enclosing emit/condition). Also add `first`/`last`/`count` converters over List for readability.

gaps.what: `{"skip": n}` is decode-only and destroys information, so any parse using it can never satisfy §7's encode(decode(bytes)) == bytes.
gaps.why: In my spec-only PART A parse, `skip` is the ONLY way past the community string, the OIDs and the values — so the round-trip bar is failed by construction, not by accident. §7 states the bar but §3 provides a field whose use makes the bar unreachable, with no warning.
gaps.proposedFix: Either forbid `skip` in any parse block referenced by a round-trippable message and require `{"bytes":{"len":n},"as":"..."}` instead, or make `skip` implicitly retain its bytes under a generated name (`_skip@<offset>`) that the encoder replays. The first is cleaner; the second keeps existing documents working. Validate-time check: a message declaring `"roundTrip": true` may not contain `skip`.

gaps.what: Listing `snmp` as a sugar layer in §2 is the grammar conceding the point, and it does not survive its own rule that sugar compiles to `bytes`.
gaps.why: §2 lists `snmp` among the sugar layers that "expand to bytes + a transport intent", but §7 says a protocol-specific code path means the grammar has failed. Given GAP-1 through GAP-8, no expansion of `snmp` into the v0 `bytes` layer exists — so a builtin `snmp` layer could only be a bespoke assembly, exactly what §7 forbids. The same is true of the `dns` entry beside it (name compression) and arguably `coap` (option deltas).
